She snarled at my dog on a walk when he got a little energetic near her but otherwise she is amazing on walks and non reactive to anything else, she briefly tried to chase one squirrel. We never fully integrated her and our dog, she has been more alert around him in the house so we mostly kept them separated. I think she would prefer to be the only pet in the home! No signs of stranger danger and she hasn’t barked at all, she’s very quiet and just whimpers for a few seconds when she’s left alone. I think she has been abused in the past, she cowers like she thinks you’re going to hit her and she is extremely responsive to “no”. She’s very eager to please. Not one accident in the house after 2 years in the shelter! I love her so much, the best girl. She is SO loving and extremely cuddly. She does come at you and is a little jumpy with big energy when she hasn’t seen you for a minute but it’s very brief and she settles quickly.

4/4/2024 Spanky Training/Handling Tips:? Drop off enrichment to help him expend some mental energy if possible before taking him out. (Frozen enrichment can be found in the white freezer located in the back sally port)? Before opening the kennel, show him your treats and ask him to “sit” and then give him a treat when he sits. If he’s excited, it  may take a few asks before he responds. Then use the treat on the other side of the loop trick to get the leash on him.? Keep treats visible as you walk and throw them on the ground for him to “find it” until you get outside or he shifts his attention to his surroundings ? If he bites at the leash, continue walking while ignoring the behavior. If you are in a contained area, intersperse dropping the leash in response to any increase in tugging. As soon as there is a slight pause or decrease in intensity, redirect him with “down” and/or “sit” and then give him a treat with verbal praise. Repeat as needed.? Start walking again, a treat + praise or throwing treat for him to "find it" every few steps ? If he starts to bite again, correct him by saying “eh” and then reset his behavior with “down” or “sit” followed by treat + praise. Then resume walking ? Once biting stops, keep him engaged and reinforce good walking with intermittent treats thrown for him to find? When un/re-leashing, first ask him to “sit” first and then give him a treat.  ** If you try to pull the leash away from him, he will tug back. If you ignore, drop the leash (he's not a runner), and redirect him with a command, then he will drop the leash to fetch the treat! ** Continue asking him to "find it" until he is leading the walk and no longer looking at you. At this point, he'll be easy on leash ** Any time you need to adjust/tighten/handle the leash, ask him to do something and reward him right as you do it (this results in him focusing on what you want him to do vs. the leash you're adjusting)

3/4/2025 Google doc:https://docs.google.com/document/d/12VRZbec5PdplO1XKaDgVG3t8xgSpf__i1z994XBE-vg/edit?usp=sharingPrimary Presenting Issues:Separation AnxietyReactivity to other dogsReactivity to strange menBackground/History:Two year old, 56 lbs, spayed maleTrazodone 100mg 2 tablets, once ever 12 hrs. Theo has been with Nelly for two monthsAverage of 4-5 hrs home alone (without human companionship)Knows sit, lay down, stay, waitTheo seems to do better with strange males in his own house compared to other environments. Nelly described some interactions with other dogs but it’s hard for me to tell if Theo was being playful or aggressive without video of it. For the moment I have asked Nelly to stop dog-to-dog interactions until Theo has some more skills and feels more confident. I am referring Nelly to Malena DeMartini website for separation anxiety help with a licenced professional. Primary Care Veterinarian: LifeLine Animal Shelter Veterinarian Food/Feeding Schedule: Daily Fresh 3 cups a day, 7am, 1pm, 7pm.Medical Issues:No known medical issuesExercise:Out for potty 5 times a day10-15 min walk three times a day30 min walk 1-2 times a dayFetch and walking around the yard 2-3 times a dayTraining:No known formal training historyEquipment:Body harness6 ft leashRecommendations:It is incredibly important to manage Theo’s environment so that he does not get a chance to rehearse the undesirable behaviors. If you see that he has already spotted an other dog approaching, move the other way to gain some distance from the other dog. It’s important to not prompt Theo to perform a cue that he is not ready to perform or has not practice under those circumstances. Remember, practice makes perfect. Practice all the suggested behaviors in different situations and environments where Theo is successful. Slowly practice outdoors as Theo’s confidence increases and starts to offer unprompted check-ins. Practice scenarios that you have experienced in the past without the distraction. Work on distance, distraction and duration as three separate levels of difficulty. See below a list of activities you can do to help Theo with his reactivity and also to meet strangers.Confidence:Sniffing GamesFind it! This is a great game to play encouraging your dog to find a treat (or toy if he has a favorite toy). Show your dog a treat or his favorite toy, and then place it out of his sight but easily accessible. Tell him to “Find it!”. Once he finds it praise enthusiastically. You can start to increase the difficulty of the game by turning off the lights, adding more treats, using boxes or even hiding treats in less conventional places like inside of a shoe. The rewards for the dog are multiple- he gets a treat or finds his toy plus a very happy handler. If issuing a toy, be sure to reward his find with some play before starting again. When multiple treats or toys are used, this particular game helps to build persistence and trust in the handler. The dog may initially find only 2 out of 3 treats, but he quickly discovers that persistence in searching when you give the “Find it!” cue pays off. He learns to believe you - there really is another one there! FreeworkIntroduction to FreeworkPlace snuffle mats and licky mats around an rea of your hours and load them with treats, yogurt, peanut butter, etc… Let your dog go in and explore the area while enjoying the amazing treats you set out for him. Don’t give him big pieces, this activity is more about the journey of finding the treats. Try using small crumbs so encourage more sniffing. You can also use your dog’s kibble for this. This game allows your dog to freely go in an area and explore. You can also do the same set-up outdoors to encourage him to sniff in situations where he might want to bark otherwise. Scatter FeedScatter Feeding Dogs: A Step-by-Step Guide To Our Favourite Calm Enrichment Activity!Why scatter feeding is beneficial for dogsScatter feeding provides a way for Theo to use his nose and calm down. You can use the same cue as “Find it!”. Do this in your back yard or even Sniffspots! Consent TestPetting Consent Tests movieParticing this form of consent testing will help Theo have some predictability when meeting strangers. Knowing that he wont be petted unless requested can be very empowering for dogs. When Theo meets strangers, please encourage your visitors to not do strong eye contact or talk to Theo at least initially. Let Theo do some freework or scatter feet for some minutes while he is adjusting to the presence of the new visitor. Communication:Teach Unprompted Attention/Auto Check-InAuto Check-In.pdfI am attaching a handout on how to do this but here is a short course on how to teach it with some demo videos: https://suzanneclothier.com/shop/autocheckin/This is very similar to the “Look at me” cue with the difference that it’s coming from the inside out where the dog is voluntarily offering attention. Puppy Politeness PokerPractice Puppy Politeness Poker by creating a list of reliable cues Theo will enthusiastically perform. Also create a list of real-life rewards that he will work for (meal time, access to a snuffle mat, opening a door, etc). Utilize those cues to give him explicit permission to access something he wants and change it up every time. This will teach Theo to slow down, listen to your request and work for what he wants. Teaches impulse control, attention and it polishes the communication between you and him. You can learn more about this concept by watching this free webinar: https://suzanneclothier.com/member_video_library/puppy-politeness-poker-webinar/Training:Teaching TouchTouch.pdfOnce Theo is able to give a “Touch” when cued in different situations, you can start using this cue during walks when you see that he spots an other dog and want to prevent him from reacting. You might need to use smellier rewards in the beginning. Practice WaitI don’t have a hand-out for wait but it sounds like Theo already knows this behavior and he just need to practice. Start small with baby steps. Take one step at a time to build distance. Once you are able to ask Theo to wait and go to a different room you can start working on duration. Once Theo is able to wait for a longer period of time you can throw in distractions like maybe closing a door and then opening it. The more you practice this, the easier it will be for him once you take it outside and introduce it in the stairs. Remember to start out with baby steps, even through Theo already has mastered “Wait” with distance, duration and distractions in-doors, you still want to start with just one step outdoors. Management:Teach 1-2-3 Treat! https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ui6dWBDdDScI wasn’t able to find any great videos of this (I should make my own lol) but basically you condition your dog to expect a treat when they hear the word “three”. If you practice this in-doors with no distractions, you eventually will be abe to do this outdoors. When you see another dog coming then you can perform the pattern that Theo already knows and he will prefer to be next to you waiting for the treat instead of reacting to the other dog. Emergency “U” turnTeaching an Emergency U Turn Portland Dog Training/ Teach an Emergency U-Turn for your Reactive Dog/ Noble Woof Dog TrainingTeaching Theo an Emergency “U” turn will help you get out of situations where he is likely to react. By practicing this, you will be able to prevent him from practicing the undesirable behavior. Scatter FeedAfter Theo has had a lot of practice with the “Find it” cue, you can do a scatter feed during walks when you see there is a dog approaching on the opposite site of the street. Please be mindful that this would be done if you are sure that the other dog is not walking towards you or wont approach you. This is meant as a management technique to prevent him from reacting to an other dog and rehearse the undesirable behavior. TouchOnce Theo learns touch, you can also do this to basically step aside and call him over buy asking him to touch. This will allow you to position him an a way where he is not facing the other dog approaching and will buy you some time while the other dog finishes crossing. Follow up:I recommend booking an in-person appointment to work on counter conditioning and desensitizing Theo to other dogs during walks and address reactivity issues. Additionally we can work practicing polite greetings with strangers. To book your next in-person appointment please visit https://loyalpawrenting.pet/ → Book Now → First Let’s Meet → Step 2: In-Home Assessment.During this 1.5 hr visit, we will work on creating a customized training, enrichment and management plan to set up Theo for success. We will also perform a Relationship Assessment Test to determine behavior patterns in your relationship with Theo. If you are interested in self-paced training I recommend taking the following course by Victoria Stillwell: https://positively.com/learning/course/help-stop-reactivity

8/21/2025 8/21/25Hi there,Here are notes about Whiskey during this week-long evaluation.  We can keep him for a few more days, possibly returning him on Sunday or Monday - still working on the logistics as we will be traveling next week and I know Tuesdays are rough and I want to continue to set him up for success as much as possible.Home set-up:Whiskey was housed in a separate room, away from our 2 resident dogs.  The room is double gated at the door - a baby gate at the threshold and a removable gate to add more distance from my resident dog's noisy eyes to the entrance of the room.  The room is on the third floor of our townhome and was set-up with cameras for additional monitoring.  The loudest the room would get would be when I was home and on work calls.  We also had an air filter running all day, on it's highest setting it can be loud, but seemed like white noise.When Whiskey needed to go out/downstairs for a walk or to go potty, our 2 residents dogs were crated and secured in a space on the main floor where Whiskey could not approach their gates directly.  The ground floor is my husband's space and where he works.  We practiced crate and rotate in our home while Whiskey was with us.Daily routine:Whiskey was taken out 3-4 times a day, depending if I went to the office.  Frequent breaks ensured he did not go potty in the house.  When at home, one of those outings would be a lunch-time or early afternoon 10-15 minute walk outside.  Whiskey was fed 2x a day, breakfast and dinner.  When working from home, I would crate him after breakfast and after his lunch-time walk, I would have him roam the room free while I continued to work. After dinner, I let Whiskey have the room on his own, uncrated.  He usually just lay on the floor and watched the door until I came back.  He would be crated overnight as he slept.Health notes:Whiskey still coughs, but there are no signs of phlegm and his nose is no longer runny/mucus-y.  His coughs happen mostly when he has just woken up or when he's walking up and down the stairs.  He is still taking doxy in the AM along with his breakfast.  He is still butt scoots on occasion.  His nose and paws are very dry though, they feel scratchy. Pus still continues to show up around his eyes, though not as much as when he first got here - but still present.  He seems to have some stiffness in his rear legs though.Eyesight:I think Whiskey can see shadows, the bigger the item the better he can maneuver around it or at least know that it's there.  He still walks down steps tentatively, but I've noticed that he prefers to walk along the stair wall, I'm assuming it helps him navigate.  He also seems to navigate better in bright light vs. a dark room.I don't know if it's eyesight or spatial distancing might be his issue or both, but sometimes he will run right into me in the backyard because he didn't realize I was right there.  He often missteps when coming to a curb. He may also flinch when you pet him on the head or under his chin because he didn't see your hand coming.General behavior:Talking - When he does make a sound, he roos or makes deep vocal grunts.  It can sound growly, but as you get to know him, it's not a growl or at least not a warning one.  He's usually vocal when we are outside or when I'm with him upstairs and playing with him and his toys.On-leash - He can pull, but he's getting better at not pulling too hard.  When he pulls, it's because something got his attention, curiosity, or interest.  Dogs walking (or barking), people walking by, strollers nearby, cats, etc.Leash-biting - Only showed leash biting when we swapped leash to a slip lead vs. leash with a clasp to his collar.  He initially attempted leash biting when you try to put the slip lead over his head. If you dangle the other end of the leash in front of him, he has tried to grab it.  To curb this, we've sprayed the slip lead with bitter apple spray and also use special treats to reward him when we can put on/take off the leash with minimal to none LB behavior.  We have also rewarded him when he lets go of the leash, if he was able to get a hold of it.  I have noticed that when the slip lead is loop is big enough where it can go over his head without him touching it on the sides of his face, it is easier and quicker to get the leash on.Potty-trained:  Whiskey is potty-trained, though it may take a few days for him to learn where he can go.  We aim to have him go out 4x a day to prevent any accidents, though 3x a day can also work where he was taken out in the morning, when I got home from work, and before going to bed.Crate-trained:  Whiskey does well in a crate and has learned to go inside on his own by tapping on the top of the crate.  Since the time he's been with us, he's only barked once in the crate, and that was during a thunderstorm. He only barked once and then was able to settle.  As he got healthier/felt safer, he midly whines when he is in the crate but still sees you near. It's more of a muffled whine, but he does not do it long and then just lays down in the crate to sleep.Treats - Whiskey is a gentle treat taker, because of his sight issues, he may need a visual cue to listen to where the treat is.  The best treats for him are smelly ones.Interactions:Other people in the home/men:  He has responded well to my husband who has given Whiskey pets and treats. My husband would come up to the baby gate where Whiskey would come up and seek pets.  Whiskey would also go up to my husband on his own when my husband was at his desk to seek pets.Kids:  We have not had him directly near kids or interact with kids.  The closest to a kid he has been was walking by the community pool on a weekend.  These were mostly small/younger kids, but a few were screaming very loudly that it made Whiskey anxious.  He pulled me towards the pool gate and attempted to try to put his head through the fence. I'm not sure if he had the intention to go through the fence or if he just couldn't tell/see a fence existed.Cats: We bumped into a neighborhood cat who was more scared of  Whiskey than Whiskey was of the cat.  Whiskey showed some interest, but I was able to call him towards me before we continued our walk.Dogs:  Both resident dogs seem curious about Whiskey, but we did not allow any type of meet and greet or walks together.  Reese (our female dog) would watch him through the baby gate+secondary gate.  When he knows she's there he will go over to the doorway.  On the second day, it seemed like he was about to make an attempt to jump on the baby gate to get a better look at Reese, but I told him "no" and got him to go back into his crate.  He hasn't tried it since.Toys and things:  Whiskey seems to prefer crinkly type toys the best, though eh has been caught licking or mouthing at sheets/towels we used to catch any potty accidents.  He's not tearing or destroying anything, just lightly mouthing/nibbling.Suggestions:If Whiskey is unable to find placement out of the shelter, it's unclear if he will regress/decline once he's back at the shelter. Considering his stressors, this could be highlly likely.  If possible, he may do well in one of the flex rooms as they have more room and tend to be a lot quieter than the runs.
